title: How many words a day to write 50,000 words in 30 days? Mac catch-up plan
metaTitle: Words a Day for 50,000 Words in 30 Days: Mac Catch-Up Plan
description: You need about 1,667 words a day to write 50,000 words in 30 days. Here is what a missed day costs, why it happens, and fixes you can use.

intro: To write 50,000 words in 30 days, you need about 1,667 words a day, or roughly 11,667 words a week. That number assumes you write on all 30 days. Any day you skip raises the target for the days that remain. This page shows the math, what a missed day costs, why the daily target slips, and fixes you can use in Word, Pages or Google Docs without buying anything.
tldr: 50,000 words over 30 days is about 1,667 words a day, every day.
Each missed writing day raises the daily number for the days left.
Skip six writing days and the target climbs to about 2,083 words a day.
Plan around 25 writing days, write a start line, and check the count each morning.

blocks.text: The math behind 1,667 words a day

Start with the two fixed numbers. The goal is 50,000 words. The window is 30 days. Divide the first by the second and you get 1,666.67. Round up and the target is 1,667 words a day. That figure assumes you write on all 30 days, including weekends, holidays and the week you travel. Few calendars leave 30 writing days untouched.

Weekly numbers are easier to hold in your head. At 1,667 words a day you need about 11,667 words each week. If you write five days a week, that is about 2,333 words on each writing day. Put that number on your calendar. It tells you what a real session needs to produce.
How the target grows when you lose writing days
The table shows the daily number for five possible counts of writing days. Every row still ends at 50,000 words by day 30. Only the number of days you can write changes.

rows: Write every day with no breaks
Three days lost to setup or travel
Four days lost in one month
A round number with five days of room
Six days lost to a busy month
blocks.caption: Words needed per writing day for 50,000 words. Simple division, rounded to the nearest word.

blocks.text: Look at the jump from 30 days to 24. You lose six days, and the daily number rises by 416 words. That is about a quarter more writing on every day you still have. A lost day is never a small problem when the target is this tight.
A worked example: one short day in week one

Say day 1 goes badly. Your target is 1,667 words and you write 900. You are 767 words behind. You could add 767 to tomorrow, which makes tomorrow 2,434 words. Or you could spread the 767 across the 29 days you have left.

Spreading is the better move. The 767 divided by 29 is about 26 words. Your new target is about 1,693 words a day. Check it the same way. You need 49,100 words over 29 days, and 49,100 divided by 29 is about 1,693. Use that number tomorrow and every day after.

The one-day catch-up feels fast, but it is hard to repeat. A 2,434 word day needs a long, clear block of time. If that block slips, you start the next day behind again. Small increases hold better than one large jump.

blocks.title: Recalculate every morning
blocks.text: Each morning, take the words still needed and divide by the writing days left, including today. Write the number on a sticky note or in the top line of your log. It takes less than a minute.
Mistakes people make with a daily word count

items: Counting calendar days instead of writing days. A rest day still sits in the divisor, so the daily number comes out too low.
Counting research and outlines as draft words. Those words only move the goal forward if they end up in the manuscript.
Mixing net and new words. Cutting 300 bad words lowers a net total but adds nothing to a new word count. Pick one method before day 1.
Setting the target and never checking the count. A number you never look at is a wish, not a target.
Stopping the moment you hit the number. A strong session is the cheapest buffer you will get.

blocks.text: Which app counts words, and what it can track

Every app here counts words, but goal features vary. Scrivener is not in the app list above, but its own blog describes a project word goal. Open Project > Show Project Targets, click the number beside Words, and enter your total. Literature and Latte says progress shows as lines in the toolbar. Check their release notes for the version you run.

Pages and Google Docs need more care. Apple's Pages 15.4 user guide mentions a word count link, but the page I read describes no word goal. See [Pages for writers](/for/writers/pages). Google Docs did not show a built-in goal in the sources I checked, and those sources disagree. Word shows a word count too, as covered in [Word for writers](/for/writers/word), but I did not confirm a goal feature. Search the Help menu for the exact name before you rely on one.
The fallback works in every app. Keep a log in a note or a spreadsheet. Write the date, the words added, and the running total. Ten lines a day is enough to see a slip before it turns into a week.

blocks.title: Check session counts early
blocks.text: Older Scrivener release notes say version 3.1.1 changed session word counts to reset even when no session target is set. Look at the session count when you start, not halfway through.
Privacy and employer rules for drafts

A contract or an employer may limit where unpublished work goes. Read the confidentiality terms before you use voice or AI tools on a manuscript, client file or internal document. Follow your employer or publisher rules on client data and unpublished work, even when a tool seems harmless. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.
Drafting by voice when typing slows you down

Speaking can be faster than typing for a first draft. Test your own rate with the [speaking vs typing test](/tools/speaking-vs-typing-test), then decide. If speaking wins for you, hold fn and dictate a rough section at the cursor. Dictation is unlimited on both the Pro and Power plans, which you can compare on the [pricing page](/pricing).

Dictated text is rough. Edit it by typing, and keep the voice yours. Lazur drafts and types text, so you still review every line. Use it for a bridge paragraph or a rough scene, not for the whole book.
Edge cases: when 1,667 is the wrong number

Some projects need a different start. A memoir with interviews may need days of reading before any draft words exist. If your first three days go to planning, start the count on day 4 and divide by 27. The method stays the same. You change the number of days, not the goal.

Nonfiction with heavy citations needs one more rule. Count the words in the manuscript, not the notes file. If the notes live in the same document, move them out before you start counting. Otherwise the total looks bigger than the draft really is.
Writing income and what a missed target costs

For many writers, the word count feeds the money. The Authors Guild's 2023 survey, covering 2022 income, found full-time authors had a median book income of $10,000. Their median total book plus author-related income was $20,000. The survey is voluntary, so read it as a rough guide, not a census.

The BLS median pay for writers and authors is $76,910 a year, based on May 2025 data. BLS figures leave out self-employed workers, and the handbook notes that many writers are self-employed or freelance. A freelancer's pay depends on deadlines, so a slipping word count can slip a deadline. It rarely costs you the whole book.
A word target is a tool. It does not write the book. It shows you early when your plan does not match your calendar. Use it to make one small decision each morning.
What to do next this week

Start with one number and one time slot. Count your real writing days, divide 50,000 by that count, and write the result on the first line of your log. Then book the first session. Gollwitzer and Sheeran's 2006 review found 94 tests of if-then plans with a medium to large effect on goal attainment (d = .65).

Treat that effect with care. Later work suggests the 2006 figure may be inflated, so do not count on it as a promise. Still, an if-then sentence takes one minute to write. Write yours tonight, put it at the top of the draft, and read it before you open email.

faq.question: How many words a day do I need to write 50,000 words in 30 days?
faq.answer: About 1,667 words a day, on all 30 days. Divide 50,000 by 30 and round up. If you write five days a week, aim for about 2,333 words on each writing day.

faq.question: What if I miss a day of my 50,000 word plan?
faq.answer: Subtract the words you wrote from that day's target and spread the gap over the days left. In the worked example, a 767 word gap on day 1 moves the target to about 1,693 a day, which is about 26 more per day.

faq.question: Does 50,000 words in 30 days count edits and cuts?
faq.answer: It depends on how you count. A net total goes down when you cut, and a new word count does not. Choose one method before day 1 and keep it for the whole month.

faq.question: Does Pages have a word goal for writers?
faq.answer: The Pages 15.4 user guide describes a word count link, but the page I read describes no word goal. Keep a log in a note or a spreadsheet until you confirm a goal feature in Pages.

faq.question: Does Scrivener have a word target?
faq.answer: Yes. According to Literature and Latte, choose Project > Show Project Targets, click the number beside Words, and enter your goal. Check the release notes for the version you run.

faq.question: Can Lazur write my 50,000 words?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts and types text when you ask, and you review every line. It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you.

costs.title: Every missed day raises the next one
costs.text: A missed day does not disappear. It moves into the days you still have, and the daily number rises. At 30 writing days the target is 1,667 words. At 24 it is 2,083. That gap is hard to close with a few extra minutes each day, so one slow week can turn into a rushed month.

costs.title: Deadlines and promises to others
costs.text: If you promised a draft to an editor, a publisher or a writing group, a missed daily number becomes a missed date. Tell them early. A new date you can meet is better than a quiet slip that surprises everyone.

costs.title: Lost momentum on the draft
costs.text: A stalled draft is harder to restart than a fresh one. When the count drops, you may start to avoid the file. Each avoided session makes the next one harder to start, and the gap grows while you wait for a better week.

costs.title: Late sessions with less energy
costs.text: A missed target often means a late session. Late sessions are tired sessions, and tired sessions tend to produce fewer words. Plan the main session for the time you have the most energy, not the time left over after email.

causes.title: The target ignores your real calendar
causes.text: A daily number built on 30 days assumes no rest days, no travel and no bad weeks. Real schedules have some of each. The plan needs the days you can write, not the days printed on the wall.

causes.title: Strong intentions with no start time
causes.text: The Gollwitzer and Sheeran abstract argues that a strong goal intention does not guarantee success. If-then plans help people start pursuing a goal, keep distractions out and drop strategies that fail. Without a start time, the first session slides, and the rest of the day slides with it.

causes.title: Editing eats the count
causes.text: Writers who revise each paragraph before moving on can write fewer new words. Cuts lower a net total. If you judge every sentence as you type, the count moves slowly and the feeling of falling behind grows. Drafting and editing are two jobs, and doing both at once makes each slower.

causes.title: Stopping when the scene gets hard
causes.text: A session often ends at the hardest point, because you do not yet know what comes next. The next morning you have to find the thread again before you write a word. That lost start costs time the daily number never counts.

causes.title: Nobody checks the count
causes.text: If the count lives only in your head, it is easy to forget on a busy day. A tally you check each morning shows a slip while it is small. Without that check, a shortfall of a few hundred words can go unnoticed for days.

fixes.title: Plan for 25 writing days, not 30
fixes.text: Set the plan at 25 writing days and the daily target is 2,000 words. That leaves five days of room for travel, illness or a bad week. You still aim for 50,000 words in a month, and the plan does not break on the first missed day.

fixes.title: Write an if-then start line
fixes.text: Write one sentence at the top of the draft. For example: If it is 7:30 a.m., then I open this file before email. Read it before each session. The sentence names a time and a first action, which is the kind of plan the if-then research tests.

fixes.title: Spread the gap, do not double up
fixes.text: When a day falls short, subtract the words you wrote from that day's target. Divide the gap by the writing days left, and add that small amount to each remaining day. Doubling up in one day is hard to repeat, so it rarely closes the gap for good.

fixes.title: Draft fast, then count new words
fixes.text: Set a rule for the session. Write forward until the timer ends, and mark gaps and typos in brackets for later. Count the new words that session added. A fast first draft gives the count something real to measure.

fixes.title: Stop mid-sentence
fixes.text: End each session in the middle of a sentence, or leave a note such as Next: the dock scene. The next session starts with a line to finish, so you never face a blank page cold. It costs nothing to do.

fixes.title: Check the count at the start of each session
fixes.text: Write the date, the words added and the new total in a log before you write anything else. A short check each morning catches a slip while it is still small. Use your app's count, or a spreadsheet if the app has no goal feature.

fixes.title: Dictate the rough draft
fixes.text: Hold fn and speak the rough version of a scene at the cursor. Test your speed first with the speaking vs typing test. Then edit by typing. Speaking may be faster for some writers, but the words still need your review.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Set the real number
plan.text: Count your writing days for the month on a calendar. Divide 50,000 by that count and round up. Write the result on the first line of your log, not the 30 day figure.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Book a fixed session
plan.text: Choose one session of about 45 minutes at the same time each day. Put it on your calendar and set an alert ten minutes before it starts.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Write the if-then line
plan.text: Put a sentence at the top of the draft that names the time and the first action. Read it before you open email, and keep it there for the whole month.

plan.label: Daily
plan.title: Check, write, stop mid-sentence
plan.text: Check the count, write for the session, then end on a note that names the next beat. Log the new words before you close the file.

plan.label: Day 7
plan.title: Review the week
plan.text: Add the week's words and compare them with the weekly number. If you are short, adjust the daily number for the next week. Do not change the goal itself.

plan.label: Missed day
plan.title: Spread the gap
plan.text: Subtract the words you wrote from that day's target. Divide the gap by the writing days left, and add the result to each remaining day.
